entities.name: Green turtle
entities.fact: Adult green sea turtles graze on seagrass and algae, which stains their fat green and gives them their name; they may live for 70 years or more.

entities.name: Manatee
entities.fact: Manatees are slow plant eaters that graze on seagrass for several hours a day and can live for 60 years or more; Snooty, a Florida manatee, lived to 69.

entities.name: Parrotfish
entities.fact: Parrotfish scrape algae from rock and dead coral with beak-like teeth, grinding up the rock and excreting it as fine white sand.

entities.name: Dugong
entities.fact: The dugong is the only fully marine mammal that lives almost entirely on seagrass, leaving tell-tale furrows through the meadows, and it can live for 70 years.

entities.name: Surgeonfish
entities.fact: Surgeonfish, or tangs, are reef grazers that crop algae all day and carry a scalpel-like blade on each side of the tail.

entities.name: Damselfish
entities.fact: Many damselfish farm their own gardens of algae on the reef, fiercely chasing away any fish, diver or turtle that comes to graze.

entities.name: Red sea urchin
entities.fact: The red sea urchin feeds on kelp off the Pacific coast of North America and can live for more than 100 years.

entities.name: Unicornfish
entities.fact: Unicornfish are large surgeonfish with a horn on the forehead that graze on brown seaweeds on Indo-Pacific reefs.

entities.name: Tuna
entities.fact: Tunas are warm-blooded, torpedo-shaped sprinters among the fastest fish in the sea; in Japan tuna is maguro, the most popular sushi fish of all.

entities.name: Yellowtail
entities.fact: Yellowtail, or hamachi, is a fast-swimming Japanese amberjack farmed in large numbers in Japan and served raw for its buttery flesh.

entities.name: Snapper
entities.fact: Snappers are warm-water reef fish prized for their firm white flesh; the red snapper of the Gulf of Mexico is the most famous, and many other fish are sold under its name.

entities.name: Grouper
entities.fact: Groupers are big-mouthed reef predators that swallow prey whole with a sudden gulp; they are a staple of Caribbean and Southeast Asian restaurants.

entities.name: Sturgeon
entities.fact: Sturgeons are armoured, shark-tailed fish older than the dinosaurs that can live for over 100 years; they are farmed for caviar now that wild Caspian stocks are protected.

entities.name: Bonito
entities.fact: Bonitos are striped, tuna-like fish of the mackerel family; in Japan 'bonito' usually means the skipjack, seared as katsuo tataki or dried into bonito flakes.

entities.name: Bluefin tuna
entities.fact: The Atlantic bluefin tuna can weigh more than 600 kilograms and is warm-blooded, keeping its muscles warmer than the sea so it can sprint after prey.

entities.name: Pacific bluefin tuna
entities.fact: The Pacific bluefin tuna is the species behind Tokyo's record new-year auctions; one sold for about 333 million yen in 2019.

entities.name: Southern bluefin tuna
entities.fact: The southern bluefin tuna was fished down to a small fraction of its original numbers and is now ranched in sea pens off South Australia.

entities.name: Yellowfin tuna
entities.fact: Yellowfin tuna, sold as ahi, is a fast, warm-water tuna with long yellow fins that is the common tuna in poke and sushi outside Japan.

entities.name: Albacore
entities.fact: Albacore, the 'white tuna' of canned tuna, has the longest pectoral fins of any tuna and is served as shiro maguro in sushi bars.

entities.name: Skipjack tuna
entities.fact: Skipjack is the most-caught tuna in the world and the one in most tins; in Japan it is katsuo, dried into bonito flakes and seared as tataki.

entities.name: Bigeye tuna
entities.fact: The bigeye tuna, with large eyes for hunting in dim deep water, is a major catch for longline fleets and is sold as sashimi-grade ahi in Hawaii.

entities.name: Little tunny
entities.fact: The little tunny, or false albacore, is the most common tuna in the Atlantic, a small, fast, scribble-patterned fish loved by fly anglers but rarely eaten.

entities.name: Atlantic bonito
entities.fact: The Atlantic bonito is a fast, striped, tuna-like schooling fish of the Atlantic and Mediterranean, eaten salted or grilled in Turkey as palamut.

entities.name: Wahoo
entities.fact: The wahoo is a long, razor-toothed member of the mackerel family and one of the fastest fish in the sea; Hawaiians call it ono, meaning delicious.

entities.name: King mackerel
entities.fact: The king mackerel, or kingfish, is a big, fast Spanish mackerel of the western Atlantic, chased by anglers off Florida and known to leap clear of the water.

entities.name: Swordfish
entities.fact: Swordfish slash at squid with a flat bill and are among the fastest fish in the sea; their meaty steaks are eaten worldwide and served raw as mekajiki in Japan.

entities.name: Conger eel
entities.fact: Conger eel, anago, is a saltwater eel simmered until soft and served with a sweet sauce in sushi; it is leaner than freshwater unagi.

entities.name: Flying fish
entities.fact: Flying fish sprint to about 60 kilometres per hour to burst from the water, then glide up to 200 metres on wing-like fins; their roe is tobiko in sushi.

entities.name: Geoduck
entities.fact: The geoduck is a huge Pacific clam with a siphon up to a metre long; it can live for more than 150 years, is farmed in Washington State and is sliced thin for sushi as mirugai.

entities.name: Greater amberjack
entities.fact: The greater amberjack, kanpachi in Japan, is a fast, powerful hunter of the open water, farmed in sea pens and served as firm, mild sashimi.

entities.name: Mahi-mahi
entities.fact: Mahi-mahi, or dorado, is a fast-growing, brilliantly coloured open-ocean fish that is among the fastest swimmers in the sea and a popular restaurant catch.

entities.name: European sea bass
entities.fact: The European sea bass, sold as branzino in restaurants, is heavily farmed in the Mediterranean and is one of Europe's favourite white fish.

entities.name: Barramundi
entities.fact: Barramundi, the Asian sea bass, is farmed widely in Australia and Southeast Asia; it starts life as a male and later changes into a female.

entities.name: Orange roughy
entities.fact: Orange roughy is a deep-sea fish that can live for more than 150 years, so it was fished out quickly after it became a restaurant favourite in the 1980s.

entities.name: Sablefish
entities.fact: Sablefish, sold as black cod, is a buttery deep-water fish of the North Pacific, famous miso-marinated, and it can live for more than 90 years.

entities.name: Pangasius
entities.fact: Pangasius, sold as basa or river cobbler, is a Vietnamese Mekong catfish farmed in vast numbers and exported as cheap white fillets.

entities.name: Japanese eel
entities.fact: The Japanese eel, unagi, cannot yet be bred commercially, so eel farms raise wild-caught glass eels in warm ponds for about a year before they are grilled as kabayaki.

entities.name: Roundnose grenadier
entities.fact: The roundnose grenadier is a deep-sea cod relative trawled at over 1,000 metres in the North Atlantic that can live for more than 50 years.

entities.name: Channel catfish
entities.fact: The channel catfish is the most farmed fish in the United States and the official state fish of several southern and midwestern states.

entities.name: Blue catfish
entities.fact: The blue catfish is the largest catfish in North America, reaching over 60 kilograms, and has become an invasive species in Chesapeake Bay.

entities.name: Flathead catfish
entities.fact: The flathead catfish is a big, mottled yellow-brown predator that eats only live prey, and is caught by 'noodling' with bare hands in the southern United States.

entities.name: Bullhead catfish
entities.fact: Bullheads are small, dark catfish of North American ponds and slow rivers that can survive in warm, low-oxygen water that kills other fish.

entities.name: Wels catfish
entities.fact: The wels catfish of European rivers can grow to over 2.5 metres and has been filmed lunging onto the bank to snatch pigeons.

entities.name: Mekong giant catfish
entities.fact: The Mekong giant catfish is one of the largest freshwater fish on Earth, reaching about 3 metres and 300 kilograms, and is critically endangered.

entities.name: Pleco
entities.fact: Plecos are armoured suckermouth catfish from South America kept to clean algae from aquariums; released into the wild, they have become pests in Texas and Florida.

entities.name: Corydoras
entities.fact: Corydoras, or cory cats, are small armoured catfish from South America that gulp air at the surface and shuffle through aquarium gravel in groups.

entities.name: Glass catfish
entities.fact: The glass catfish of Southeast Asia is so transparent you can see its bones and organs, and it turns milky white when it dies.

entities.name: Electric catfish
entities.fact: The electric catfish of African rivers can deliver shocks of about 350 volts and was pictured in ancient Egyptian tomb art.

entities.name: Walking catfish
entities.fact: The walking catfish can breathe air and wriggle overland between ponds on wet nights, and has spread across Florida since escaping from fish farms in the 1960s.

entities.name: Redtail catfish
entities.fact: The redtail catfish of the Amazon has a bright orange-red tail and grows well over a metre, a giant that aquarists often regret buying.

entities.name: Upside-down catfish
entities.fact: The upside-down catfish of the Congo basin habitually swims belly-up to feed at the surface, and its belly is darker than its back as a result.

entities.name: Bristlenose pleco
entities.fact: The bristlenose pleco is a small armoured catfish whose males grow a bush of fleshy tentacles on the snout; it is a popular aquarium algae eater.

entities.name: Tiger shovelnose catfish
entities.fact: The tiger shovelnose catfish of South America has a long flat snout and bold black stripes, and can grow to over a metre long.

entities.name: Piraíba
entities.fact: The piraíba is the giant catfish of the Amazon, reaching about 3 metres and more than 150 kilograms, the largest catfish in the Americas.

entities.name: Candiru
entities.fact: The candiru is a tiny, slender Amazon catfish that slips under the gill covers of larger fish to drink their blood, and is feared far out of proportion to its size.

entities.name: Hardhead catfish
entities.fact: The hardhead catfish is a sea catfish of the Gulf of Mexico whose males carry the marble-sized eggs in their mouths for about two months.

entities.name: Gafftopsail catfish
entities.fact: The gafftopsail catfish is a sea catfish of the western Atlantic with long, sail-like fin filaments and venomous spines.

entities.name: Striped eel catfish
entities.fact: The striped eel catfish is a venomous marine catfish of Indo-Pacific reefs whose young swarm in tight, rolling balls for protection.

entities.name: African sharptooth catfish
entities.fact: The African sharptooth catfish can breathe air and crawl between pools, and is farmed widely across Africa and Asia as a cheap protein.

entities.name: Pictus catfish
entities.fact: The pictus catfish is a spotted, long-whiskered aquarium catfish from the Amazon and Orinoco whose barbels can be as long as its body.

entities.name: Otocinclus
entities.fact: Otocinclus, or 'otos', are tiny suckermouth catfish from South America, kept in aquariums to graze algae and barely 4 centimetres long.

entities.name: Striped Raphael catfish
entities.fact: The striped Raphael catfish, a 'talking catfish', squeaks by grinding its pectoral spines and is armoured with a row of sharp plates along each side.

entities.name: Banjo catfish
entities.fact: The banjo catfish is a flat, lumpy South American catfish shaped like a banjo that lies buried in sand and leaf litter by day.

entities.name: Pygmy corydoras
entities.fact: The pygmy corydoras is a 2.5-centimetre armoured catfish from Brazil that, unlike its relatives, swims in mid-water in shoals.

entities.name: Goonch
entities.fact: The goonch, or giant devil catfish, is a huge, mottled catfish of South Asian rivers, blamed in reports from the Kali River for attacks on bathers.

entities.name: Wallago
entities.fact: The wallago, or freshwater shark of South Asia, is a long, big-mouthed predatory catfish that can exceed 1.5 metres.

entities.name: Madtom
entities.fact: Madtoms are tiny North American catfish, mostly under 10 centimetres, with venom glands at the base of their pectoral spines that give a painful sting.

entities.name: Zebra pleco
entities.fact: The zebra pleco, a striking black-and-white striped catfish, lives only in a stretch of Brazil's Xingu River and is threatened by the Belo Monte dam.

entities.name: Synodontis catfish
entities.fact: Synodontis catfish of Africa are called squeakers because they chirp by rubbing their pectoral spines; the featherfin squeaker is an aquarium favourite.

entities.name: Moray eel
entities.fact: Moray eels have a second set of jaws in the throat that shoots forward to drag prey down, and their gaping mouths are simply how they breathe.

entities.name: Electric eel
entities.fact: The electric eel is not a true eel but a South American knifefish that can deliver shocks of up to about 860 volts, enough to stun a horse.

entities.name: Garden eel
entities.fact: Garden eels live in colonies on sandy slopes, each in its own burrow, swaying up into the current like grass and sinking out of sight when anything approaches.

entities.name: Pelican eel
entities.fact: The gulper eel, or pelican eel, lives in the deep sea with a mouth far bigger than its body, which it can balloon open to engulf prey.

entities.name: Ribbon eel
entities.fact: The ribbon eel is a thin moray with flared nostrils that starts life black, turns electric blue and yellow as a male and then becomes a yellow female.

entities.name: European eel
entities.fact: The European eel spawns in the Sargasso Sea, its young drifting across the Atlantic to Europe's rivers; one captive eel lived for more than 80 years.

entities.name: American eel
entities.fact: The American eel also spawns in the Sargasso Sea, and its transparent 'glass eel' young are worth thousands of dollars a kilogram to Asian eel farms.

entities.name: Green moray
entities.fact: The green moray of the Caribbean is actually brown; a coat of yellow mucus over its skin makes it look green.

entities.name: Giant moray
entities.fact: The giant moray can reach 3 metres and is the heaviest moray; it has been filmed hunting cooperatively with groupers on Red Sea reefs.

entities.name: Snowflake moray
entities.fact: The snowflake moray has blunt, pebble-like teeth for crushing crabs and shrimp, and is a popular aquarium moray.

entities.name: Snake eel
entities.fact: Snake eels burrow tail-first into sand with a hard, pointed tail tip and are often mistaken for sea snakes when they swim.

entities.name: Spotted garden eel
entities.fact: The spotted garden eel lives in colonies of hundreds on Indo-Pacific sand slopes, each eel anchored tail-first in its own burrow.

entities.name: Freshwater eel
entities.fact: Freshwater eels spend most of their lives in rivers and lakes, then make a single journey to the sea to spawn and die.

entities.name: Zebra moray
entities.fact: The zebra moray, banded in dark brown and white, has flat crushing teeth and feeds almost entirely on crabs and sea urchins.

entities.name: Snipe eel
entities.fact: Snipe eels are thread-thin deep-sea eels with long, bird-like jaws that curve apart at the tips and cannot fully close.

entities.name: Short-finned eel
entities.fact: The short-finned eel of Australia and New Zealand migrates thousands of kilometres to spawn in the Coral Sea.

entities.name: New Zealand longfin eel
entities.fact: The New Zealand longfin eel is one of the largest and longest-lived freshwater eels; females can live for more than 60 years before heading to sea to spawn once.

entities.name: Giant mottled eel
entities.fact: The giant mottled eel is the largest freshwater eel, reaching about 2 metres, and ranges from East Africa to Polynesia.

entities.name: European conger
entities.fact: The European conger is one of the largest eels, reaching about 3 metres and more than 100 kilograms, and lurks in wrecks and rocky holes.

entities.name: Cutthroat eel
entities.fact: Cutthroat eels are deep-sea eels named for the slit-like gill openings low on the throat, found on the seabed down to several thousand metres.

entities.name: Pike conger
entities.fact: The daggertooth pike conger is a fanged eel of Indo-Pacific coasts eaten in Japan as hamo, famously in Kyoto in summer.

entities.name: Honeycomb moray
entities.fact: The honeycomb moray, or laced moray, is a large white moray covered in black honeycomb spots, common on Indo-Pacific reefs.

entities.name: Mediterranean moray
entities.fact: The Mediterranean moray was a Roman delicacy, kept in seaside fish ponds by wealthy Romans.

entities.name: Dragon moray
entities.fact: The dragon moray has curved fangs and horn-like nostril tubes, making it one of the most striking eels of Indo-Pacific reefs.

entities.name: Sawtooth eel
entities.fact: Sawtooth eels are small deep-sea eels with saw-like rows of teeth, drifting in the midwater of all the oceans.

entities.name: Spaghetti eel
entities.fact: Spaghetti eels are extremely thin, worm-like eels of the Indo-Pacific that burrow in sand and are found in rivers as well as the sea.

entities.name: Bobtail snipe eel
entities.fact: The bobtail snipe eel is a stubby, dart-shaped deep-sea eel with long thin jaws, found in the dark waters below 1,000 metres.

entities.name: Fangtooth moray
entities.fact: The fangtooth moray, with glassy, needle-like teeth and a bright yellow head, lives in the warmer rocky waters of the eastern Atlantic, including the Canaries and Madeira.

entities.name: Chain moray
entities.fact: The chain moray of the Caribbean, patterned with yellow chain links, can leave the water to hunt crabs on rocks at low tide.

entities.name: Slender giant moray
entities.fact: The slender giant moray is the longest eel in the world, reaching about 4 metres, and lives in muddy estuaries of the Indo-Pacific.

entities.name: Blue whale
entities.fact: The blue whale is the largest animal ever known to have lived, reaching about 30 metres, and its earwax layers show it can live for 90 years or more.

entities.name: Whale shark
entities.fact: The whale shark is the largest fish in the sea, reaching up to about 18 metres, yet it feeds on plankton and small fish sieved through its gills.

entities.name: Humpback whale
entities.fact: Humpback whales grow to about 16 metres, the males sing long, complex songs, and they can live for 80 years or more.

entities.name: Sperm whale
entities.fact: The sperm whale is the largest toothed predator on Earth, with males reaching about 20 metres, diving more than 2 kilometres for squid and living 70 years or more.

entities.name: Giant squid
entities.fact: The giant squid can reach about 12 metres including its two long feeding tentacles and has eyes the size of dinner plates.

entities.name: Basking shark
entities.fact: The basking shark is the second-largest fish, growing to about 12 metres, and swims slowly with its huge mouth open to filter plankton.

entities.name: Orca
entities.fact: Orcas, or killer whales, are the largest dolphins, with big males reaching about 9 metres; females can live well past 80, leading their pods as grandmothers.

entities.name: Fin whale
entities.fact: The fin whale is the second-largest animal, reaching about 26 metres, was nicknamed the 'greyhound of the sea' for its speed, and can live for about 90 years.

entities.name: Grey whale
entities.fact: The grey whale grows to about 15 metres, makes one of the longest migrations of any mammal between Mexico and the Arctic, and can live for more than 50 years.

entities.name: Bowhead whale
entities.fact: The bowhead whale reaches about 18 metres, has the thickest blubber of any animal and can live for more than 200 years.

entities.name: Minke whale
entities.fact: Minke whales are the smallest of the rorquals but still reach about 10 metres, and they are the whales most often hunted today.

entities.name: Lion's mane jellyfish
entities.fact: The lion's mane jellyfish has tentacles that can trail more than 30 metres; one washed up in Massachusetts Bay in 1870 is among the longest animals ever recorded.

entities.name: Colossal squid
entities.fact: The colossal squid of the Southern Ocean is the heaviest invertebrate and is thought to reach about 10 metres; its eyes are the largest of any animal.

entities.name: Right whale
entities.fact: Right whales grow to about 15 to 18 metres and can live for 70 years or more; whalers named them the 'right' whale to hunt because they floated when killed.

entities.name: Sei whale
entities.fact: The sei whale reaches about 20 metres and is one of the fastest great whales, able to sprint at around 50 kilometres per hour.

entities.name: Oarfish
entities.fact: The giant oarfish is the longest bony fish, measured at about 8 metres and reported far longer, and is thought to be behind many sea-serpent legends.

entities.name: Bryde's whale
entities.fact: Bryde's whale reaches about 15 metres and, unlike most great whales, stays in warm tropical waters all year round.

entities.name: North Atlantic right whale
entities.fact: The North Atlantic right whale reaches about 16 metres and is one of the most endangered whales, with only a few hundred left.

entities.name: Southern right whale
entities.fact: The southern right whale grows to about 15 to 18 metres and gathers to breed off Argentina, South Africa and Australia, where it is watched from shore.

entities.name: Northern bottlenose whale
entities.fact: The northern bottlenose whale is a bulbous-headed beaked whale of the North Atlantic that reaches almost 10 metres and can dive for over an hour.

entities.name: Baird's beaked whale
entities.fact: Baird's beaked whale is the largest beaked whale, reaching about 12 metres, and is still hunted off Japan.

entities.name: Giant siphonophore
entities.fact: The giant siphonophore Praya dubia is a deep-sea colony of linked individuals that can stretch 40 metres or more, longer than a blue whale.

entities.name: Arnoux's beaked whale
entities.fact: Arnoux's beaked whale is the Southern Ocean counterpart of Baird's beaked whale, reaching nearly 10 metres and diving under the Antarctic ice.

entities.name: Omura's whale
entities.fact: Omura's whale was only identified as a species in 2003; it reaches about 12 metres and was first filmed alive off Madagascar in 2015.

entities.name: Rice's whale
entities.fact: Rice's whale, named as a species in 2021, reaches about 12 metres and lives only in the Gulf of Mexico, where fewer than 100 survive.

entities.name: Pyrosome
entities.fact: The giant pyrosome is a glowing, tube-shaped colony of tiny animals that can grow 20 metres long, big enough for a diver to swim inside.

entities.name: North Pacific right whale
entities.fact: The North Pacific right whale reaches about 18 metres and is among the rarest whales, with perhaps only a few dozen left in the eastern Pacific.

entities.name: Antarctic minke whale
entities.fact: The Antarctic minke whale reaches almost 11 metres and feeds on krill at the edge of the sea ice.

entities.name: Bootlace worm
entities.fact: The bootlace worm is a ribbon worm of North Sea shores; one found in Scotland in 1864 measured about 55 metres, the longest animal ever recorded.

entities.name: Sailfish
entities.fact: The sailfish is widely held to be the fastest fish in the sea, raising its huge dorsal sail when it herds sardines into tight balls.

entities.name: Marlin
entities.fact: Marlins are big, spear-nosed billfish among the fastest fish in the ocean; Hemingway's The Old Man and the Sea is the story of a fight with a giant marlin.

entities.name: Mako shark
entities.fact: The shortfin mako is the fastest shark, a warm-blooded sprinter that can leap several metres out of the water when hooked.

entities.name: Great white shark
entities.fact: Great white sharks can launch themselves clear of the water in high-speed attacks on seals, a behaviour famous off South Africa's Seal Island.

entities.name: Blue marlin
entities.fact: The Atlantic blue marlin can top 4 metres and is one of the fastest, hardest-fighting fish in the sea; females grow far larger than males.

entities.name: Black marlin
entities.fact: The black marlin of the Indo-Pacific is often claimed to be the fastest fish of all, and its rigid pectoral fins cannot be folded flat against the body.

entities.name: Barracuda
entities.fact: The great barracuda is a fast, torpedo-shaped ambush hunter with fang-like teeth, able to burst at high speed to snatch passing fish.

entities.name: Blue shark
entities.fact: The blue shark is a slender, fast open-ocean shark that roams across entire ocean basins, and is the most heavily fished shark in the world.

entities.name: Tarpon
entities.fact: The tarpon is a big, fast silver game fish famous for its spectacular leaps when hooked, and it can gulp air at the surface with a lung-like swim bladder.

entities.name: Striped marlin
entities.fact: The striped marlin hunts in packs off Baja California, where it herds sardine bait balls at high speed and lights up its stripes as it attacks.

entities.name: Bonefish
entities.fact: The bonefish is the 'grey ghost' of tropical flats, a shy, fast-sprinting fish that can strip line from a fly reel in seconds.

entities.name: White marlin
entities.fact: The white marlin is the smallest Atlantic marlin, a fast, acrobatic billfish prized by anglers off the US east coast.

entities.name: Salmon shark
entities.fact: The salmon shark of the North Pacific is a warm-blooded relative of the great white, among the fastest of all sharks, that hunts salmon off Alaska.

entities.name: Shortbill spearfish
entities.fact: The shortbill spearfish is a slim, fast billfish of the Pacific with a bill barely longer than its lower jaw.

entities.name: Greenland shark
entities.fact: The Greenland shark is the longest-lived vertebrate known; radiocarbon dating of eye lenses suggests one female could be around 400 years old.

entities.name: Ocean quahog
entities.fact: The ocean quahog is a cold-water clam; one dredged off Iceland in 2006, nicknamed Ming, was 507 years old, the oldest animal whose age has been precisely measured.

entities.name: Giant clam
entities.fact: Giant clams can live for more than 100 years, growing over a metre across, and get much of their food from algae living in their colourful mantle.

entities.name: Lobster
entities.fact: American lobsters keep growing and moulting all their lives and are thought to be able to live for more than 50 years, possibly to 100.

entities.name: Loggerhead turtle
entities.fact: The loggerhead sea turtle has a huge head and powerful jaws for crushing conchs and crabs, and can live for 70 years or more.

entities.name: Coral
entities.fact: Corals are colonies of tiny animals that can live for centuries; some large boulder corals on reefs today are hundreds of years old.

entities.name: Beluga whale
entities.fact: Belugas are white Arctic whales nicknamed 'sea canaries' for their chirps and whistles; counting tooth layers shows they can live for 70 years or more.

entities.name: Rockfish
entities.fact: Rockfishes of the North Pacific are among the longest-lived fish; several species live well past 100 years, and the rougheye may reach 200.

entities.name: Brain coral
entities.fact: Brain corals grow only a few millimetres a year, so a large colony on a Caribbean reef can be several hundred years old.

entities.name: Saltwater crocodile
entities.fact: The saltwater crocodile is the largest living reptile, swims far out to sea between islands, and can live for 70 years or more.

entities.name: Rougheye rockfish
entities.fact: The rougheye rockfish is one of the longest-lived fish known, with individuals aged at more than 200 years from the growth rings in their ear bones.

entities.name: Yelloweye rockfish
entities.fact: The yelloweye rockfish of the North Pacific grows slowly and can live for more than 100 years, which makes it very easy to overfish.

entities.name: Black coral
entities.fact: Black corals grow so slowly that a colony sampled off Hawaii was found to be more than 4,000 years old, among the oldest living animals.

entities.name: Giant barrel sponge
entities.fact: The giant barrel sponge of Caribbean reefs, the 'redwood of the reef', can live for more than 2,000 years.

entities.name: Pacific halibut
entities.fact: The Pacific halibut can live for more than 50 years and reach over 200 kilograms; the oldest on record was 55.

entities.name: Beluga sturgeon
entities.fact: The beluga sturgeon of the Caspian and Black Seas can live for more than 100 years and is the source of the most expensive caviar.

entities.name: Cold-seep tubeworm
entities.fact: Tubeworms at cold seeps in the Gulf of Mexico grow so slowly that some are estimated to be more than 200 years old, among the longest-lived of all animals.

entities.name: Glass sponge
entities.fact: Glass sponges build skeletons of silica; one giant glass sponge from the East China Sea has been estimated at about 11,000 years old, perhaps the oldest animal on Earth.

entities.name: Neon tetra
entities.fact: The neon tetra, with its electric blue stripe over red, grows to only about 3 centimetres and is one of the most popular aquarium fish, with millions bred each year.

entities.name: Pygmy seahorse
entities.fact: Pygmy seahorses are mostly under 2.5 centimetres long and so well camouflaged on sea fans and corals that the first was found only when its host fan was collected.

entities.name: Zebrafish
entities.fact: The zebrafish, a striped minnow about 3 to 4 centimetres long, is one of science's favourite lab animals because its transparent embryos develop in full view.

entities.name: Paedocypris
entities.fact: Paedocypris progenetica, from the peat swamps of Sumatra, matures at under 8 millimetres and is among the smallest fish known.

entities.name: Medaka
entities.fact: The medaka, or Japanese rice fish, is a 3-centimetre fish that became the first vertebrate to mate and lay eggs in space, aboard the space shuttle in 1994.

entities.name: Dwarf seahorse
entities.fact: The dwarf seahorse of Florida's seagrass beds is about 2.5 centimetres long and was once listed as the slowest-moving fish in the world.

entities.name: White Cloud Mountain minnow
entities.fact: The White Cloud Mountain minnow is a 4-centimetre fish discovered in 1932 on a mountain near Guangzhou, now almost extinct in the wild while thriving in aquariums.

entities.name: Neon goby
entities.fact: The neon goby is a 4-centimetre Caribbean cleaner fish with a blue stripe that picks parasites from much larger fish at cleaning stations.

entities.name: Ember tetra
entities.fact: The ember tetra is a fiery orange fish from Brazil's Araguaia river basin that grows to only about 2 centimetres.

entities.name: Chili rasbora
entities.fact: The chili rasbora of Borneo's blackwater streams is a brilliant red fish barely 2 centimetres long, one of the smallest aquarium fish.

entities.name: Celestial pearl danio
entities.fact: The celestial pearl danio, a 2-centimetre fish spangled with pearly spots, was found in Myanmar in 2006 and caused such a craze that it was nearly collected to extinction.

entities.name: Endler's livebearer
entities.fact: Endler's livebearer is a tiny, brilliantly coloured relative of the guppy from Venezuela, with males under 3 centimetres long.

entities.name: Bargibant's pygmy seahorse
entities.fact: Bargibant's pygmy seahorse grows to about 2 centimetres and lives only on Muricella sea fans, matching their colour and knobbly texture so well it was found by accident in 1969.

entities.name: Glowlight tetra
entities.fact: The glowlight tetra is a 3-to-4-centimetre fish from Guyana with a glowing orange-red stripe down its side.

entities.name: Least killifish
entities.fact: The least killifish is one of the smallest fish in North America, a 2-to-3-centimetre livebearer of the southeastern United States, and not a true killifish.

entities.name: Clown killifish
entities.fact: The clown killifish is a 3-centimetre West African fish with a banded body and a rocket-flame tail that spends its life just under the surface.

entities.name: Bumblebee goby
entities.fact: The bumblebee goby is a banded black-and-yellow goby of Southeast Asian estuaries that grows to under 4 centimetres.

entities.name: Yellow clown goby
entities.fact: The yellow clown goby is a 3.5-centimetre reef fish that lives among the branches of Acropora corals and produces a bitter skin mucus to deter predators.

entities.name: Sparkling gourami
entities.fact: The sparkling gourami is a 4-centimetre fish from Southeast Asia that makes audible croaking sounds when courting or fighting.

entities.name: Dwarf pencilfish
entities.fact: The dwarf pencilfish is a slender 3.5-centimetre fish of Amazon blackwater streams with bold horizontal stripes.

entities.name: Scarlet badis
entities.fact: The scarlet badis is a 2-centimetre fish from India with scarlet and blue bars, one of the smallest perch-like fish.

entities.name: Denise's pygmy seahorse
entities.fact: Denise's pygmy seahorse is a 2-centimetre orange seahorse found on sea fans across the Coral Triangle, named after the photographer Denise Tackett.

entities.name: Stout infantfish
entities.fact: The stout infantfish of the Great Barrier Reef matures at about 7 to 8 millimetres and weighs about a milligram, one of the smallest and lightest vertebrates.

entities.name: Dwarf pygmy goby
entities.fact: The dwarf pygmy goby of Philippine mangrove streams is about 1 centimetre long as an adult and was long considered the smallest fish in the world.

entities.name: Trimmatom nanus
entities.fact: Trimmatom nanus, a goby of the Chagos Islands and Maldives, matures at under 1 centimetre and held the record as the smallest vertebrate from 1981 to 2004.

entities.name: Pygmy sunfish
entities.fact: Pygmy sunfishes of the southeastern United States are 2-to-3-centimetre swamp fish, not true sunfish, that flash iridescent blue when breeding.

entities.name: Least darter
entities.fact: The least darter is one of the smallest freshwater fish in North America, a 4-centimetre perch relative of weedy streams and lakes.

entities.name: Satomi's pygmy seahorse
entities.fact: Satomi's pygmy seahorse, from Indonesia, is about 1.4 centimetres long and is the smallest known seahorse.

entities.name: Pontoh's pygmy seahorse
entities.fact: Pontoh's pygmy seahorse is a free-living pygmy seahorse of about 1.7 centimetres that clings to algae and hydroids rather than sea fans.

entities.name: Seven-figure pygmy goby
entities.fact: The seven-figure pygmy goby, a 2-centimetre reef fish, has the shortest lifespan of any vertebrate, living for about two months.

entities.name: Green neon tetra
entities.fact: The green neon tetra is a 2.5-centimetre relative of the neon tetra from the upper Orinoco and Rio Negro with a blue-green stripe.

entities.name: Dwarf rasbora
entities.fact: The dwarf rasbora, Boraras maculatus, is a 2-centimetre spotted fish of Malaysian peat swamps.

entities.name: Danionella cerebrum
entities.fact: Danionella cerebrum, a transparent 12-millimetre fish from Myanmar, makes drumming sounds as loud as a pneumatic drill and has the smallest known vertebrate brain.

entities.name: Clownfish
entities.fact: Clownfish live unharmed among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones, protected by a mucus coat, and every clownfish is born male, with the largest becoming the female.

entities.name: Ocellaris clownfish
entities.fact: The ocellaris clownfish is the orange, three-barred fish made famous as Nemo; the film's success made it one of the most traded reef fish in the world.

entities.name: Orange clownfish
entities.fact: The orange clownfish, or percula, looks almost identical to the ocellaris but has thicker black edges to its white bars, and lives around New Guinea and the Great Barrier Reef.

entities.name: Garibaldi
entities.fact: The garibaldi is a bright orange damselfish of California's kelp forests, the state's official marine fish, and the males fiercely guard nests of red algae.

entities.name: Sergeant major
entities.fact: The sergeant major is a striped damselfish found on reefs around the world, named for the stripes on a sergeant's sleeve; it swarms around divers for crumbs.

entities.name: Maroon clownfish
entities.fact: The maroon clownfish is the largest clownfish, up to about 17 centimetres, with cheek spines and a female far bigger and more aggressive than her mate.

entities.name: Tomato clownfish
entities.fact: The tomato clownfish is a red-orange anemonefish with a single white head bar that lives in bubble-tip anemones in the western Pacific.

entities.name: Clark's anemonefish
entities.fact: Clark's anemonefish is the least fussy clownfish, able to live in all ten species of host anemone, and ranges from the Persian Gulf to Japan.

entities.name: Pink skunk clownfish
entities.fact: The pink skunk clownfish is a pale pink anemonefish with a white stripe along its back, like a skunk, living in magnificent anemones.

entities.name: Blue-green chromis
entities.fact: The blue-green chromis is a shimmering damselfish that hovers in large shoals above branching corals, darting in when danger threatens.

entities.name: Blue devil damselfish
entities.fact: The blue devil damselfish, a brilliant electric-blue fish of the western Pacific, is a hardy aquarium favourite with a devilish temper for its size.

entities.name: Domino damselfish
entities.fact: The three-spot dascyllus, or domino damsel, is a black damselfish with three white spots that often shelters in anemones as a juvenile.

entities.name: Humbug dascyllus
entities.fact: The humbug dascyllus is a small black-and-white banded damselfish that lives in tight groups inside branching Acropora corals.

entities.name: Yellowtail blue damsel
entities.fact: The yellowtail blue damsel is a deep blue damselfish with a bright yellow tail, one of the most popular and peaceful damselfish for aquariums.

entities.name: Saddleback clownfish
entities.fact: The saddleback clownfish has a white saddle on its back rather than a full bar, and lives in anemones on open sand rather than on the reef.

entities.name: Cinnamon clownfish
entities.fact: The cinnamon clownfish, or fire clownfish, is a dark red-brown anemonefish with one white head bar and a bluish tint, from the western Pacific.

entities.name: Two-banded anemonefish
entities.fact: The Red Sea clownfish, with two white bars on an orange body, is found only in the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.

entities.name: Sebae clownfish
entities.fact: The sebae clownfish is a dark anemonefish with a yellow tail and two white bars from the northern Indian Ocean; many fish sold under its name are actually Clark's.

entities.name: Blue chromis
entities.fact: The blue chromis is a brilliant blue Caribbean damselfish that feeds on plankton in open water above the reef.

entities.name: Beaugregory
entities.fact: The beaugregory is a Caribbean damselfish, yellow below and blue above as a juvenile, that fiercely defends a small patch of reef.

entities.name: Bicolor damselfish
entities.fact: The bicolor damselfish of the Caribbean is dark in front and pale behind, and tends algae gardens that it guards from other grazers.

entities.name: Jewel damselfish
entities.fact: The jewel damselfish of Indo-Pacific reefs is spangled with tiny blue spots as a juvenile, and the adult farms a turf of red algae.

entities.name: Mediterranean damselfish
entities.fact: The Mediterranean damselfish is the only damselfish in the Mediterranean, a dark fish whose juveniles are brilliant blue, common in shoals above rocks.

entities.name: Blacksmith
entities.fact: The blacksmith is a blue-grey damselfish of California's kelp forests that shelters in rock crevices at night and feeds on plankton by day.

entities.name: Wide-band anemonefish
entities.fact: The wide-band anemonefish lives only around Lord Howe Island and eastern Australia, with wide white bars that merge on some fish.

entities.name: Allard's clownfish
entities.fact: Allard's clownfish is a dark anemonefish with two white bars and a yellow tail found only off East Africa, from Kenya to South Africa.

entities.name: White-bonnet anemonefish
entities.fact: The white-bonnet anemonefish, with a white cap on its head, is a natural hybrid between the orange skunk clownfish and the orange-fin anemonefish.

entities.name: Three-band anemonefish
entities.fact: The three-band anemonefish lives only in the Marshall Islands, where some individuals turn almost completely black.

entities.name: Oman anemonefish
entities.fact: The Oman anemonefish is found only along the coast of Oman, where it lives in anemones on rocky reefs.

entities.name: Dusky farmerfish
entities.fact: The dusky farmerfish is a damselfish that cultivates a single species of red alga in its territory, weeding out everything else, in one of the only known cases of farming by a fish.

entities.name: Spiny chromis
entities.fact: The spiny chromis of the Great Barrier Reef is unusual among reef fish in that both parents guard their young for weeks after hatching.

entities.name: McCulloch's anemonefish
entities.fact: McCulloch's anemonefish is a dark clownfish with a white face found only at Lord Howe and Norfolk Islands, one of the most restricted ranges of any clownfish.

entities.name: Wrasse
entities.fact: Wrasses are a huge family of colourful reef fish, many of which start life as females and later change into brightly coloured males.

entities.name: Cleaner wrasse
entities.fact: The bluestreak cleaner wrasse runs cleaning stations where big fish queue to have parasites picked off, and it passed the mirror self-recognition test in 2019.

entities.name: Napoleon wrasse
entities.fact: The humphead wrasse is the largest wrasse, up to about 2 metres and 190 kilograms, with thick lips and a bump on its forehead; it is endangered by the live reef-fish trade.

entities.name: Bumphead parrotfish
entities.fact: The bumphead parrotfish is the biggest parrotfish, up to about 1.3 metres, and rams its forehead into coral to break off chunks to eat.

entities.name: Hogfish
entities.fact: The hogfish of the western Atlantic roots in sand with its long pig-like snout and is prized by spearfishers for its taste.

entities.name: Stoplight parrotfish
entities.fact: The stoplight parrotfish of the Caribbean changes from a mottled red-and-brown female phase to a green male with a yellow spot, like a traffic light.

entities.name: Ballan wrasse
entities.fact: The ballan wrasse is the largest wrasse in British waters, used in salmon farms to eat sea lice off the salmon.

entities.name: Cuckoo wrasse
entities.fact: The cuckoo wrasse male is one of Britain's most colourful fish, vivid blue and orange, while the female is pink; all start life as females.

entities.name: California sheephead
entities.fact: The California sheephead is a big-toothed wrasse of kelp forests that crushes sea urchins; all start life as females and the largest turn into black-and-red males.

entities.name: Tautog
entities.fact: The tautog, or blackfish, is a chunky wrasse of the US east coast that sleeps so soundly on the bottom at night that divers can pick it up.

entities.name: Bluehead wrasse
entities.fact: The bluehead wrasse of the Caribbean can change from female to male in days, and the big blue-headed males defend spawning sites.

entities.name: Queen parrotfish
entities.fact: The queen parrotfish of the Caribbean sleeps at night inside a cocoon of mucus that it secretes, which may hide its scent from predators.

entities.name: Blue parrotfish
entities.fact: The blue parrotfish is a uniform powder-blue Caribbean parrotfish that spends most of its day grinding sand and rock for algae.

entities.name: Six-line wrasse
entities.fact: The six-line wrasse is a tiny purple-and-orange striped wrasse from Indo-Pacific reefs that hunts pests such as flatworms in aquariums.

entities.name: Moon wrasse
entities.fact: The moon wrasse, or lunar wrasse, is a green-and-blue wrasse with a yellow crescent on the tail, common on reefs across the Indo-Pacific.

entities.name: Harlequin tuskfish
entities.fact: The harlequin tuskfish has bright blue tusk-like teeth and orange bands, and uses the teeth to crush shellfish on Indo-Pacific reefs.

entities.name: Corkwing wrasse
entities.fact: The corkwing wrasse of European coasts builds a nest of seaweed in a rock crevice, which the male guards until the eggs hatch.

entities.name: Goldsinny
entities.fact: The goldsinny is a small orange-brown wrasse of European rocky shores, now farmed as a cleaner fish to eat lice off farmed salmon.

entities.name: Cunner
entities.fact: The cunner is a small wrasse of the northwest Atlantic that becomes torpid in winter, hiding in crevices and barely moving in the cold.

entities.name: Bird wrasse
entities.fact: The bird wrasse has a long, curved beak-like snout that it uses to pluck small animals from crevices on Indo-Pacific reefs.

entities.name: Fairy wrasse
entities.fact: Fairy wrasses are small, dazzling wrasses of Indo-Pacific reefs; males flash their colours in courtship displays, and new species are still being named.

entities.name: Princess parrotfish
entities.fact: The princess parrotfish is a Caribbean parrotfish whose males are blue-green with pink stripes, and it grazes in mixed schools over the reef.

entities.name: Midnight parrotfish
entities.fact: The midnight parrotfish is a dark blue Caribbean parrotfish with bright blue markings on its head that often grazes in schools with other species.

entities.name: Rainbow parrotfish
entities.fact: The rainbow parrotfish is the largest parrotfish in the Atlantic, up to about 1.2 metres, with a coppery body and green fins, and its young grow up in mangroves.

entities.name: Dragon wrasse
entities.fact: The dragon wrasse, or rockmover, flips over rocks with its mouth to find prey; as a juvenile it mimics a drifting piece of seaweed.

entities.name: Slingjaw wrasse
entities.fact: The slingjaw wrasse can shoot its jaws forward to half its body length to snatch prey, the most extreme jaw protrusion of any fish.

entities.name: Blackspot tuskfish
entities.fact: The blackspot tuskfish was filmed on the Great Barrier Reef smashing clams against a rock anvil, one of the first documented cases of tool use in a fish.

entities.name: Pearly razorfish
entities.fact: The pearly razorfish dives headfirst into sand to escape danger, and can even swim short distances beneath the sand.

entities.name: Rock cook
entities.fact: The rock cook is a small wrasse of European waters that cleans parasites from other fish, and is used to de-louse farmed salmon.

entities.name: Señorita
entities.fact: The señorita is a slim, cigar-shaped wrasse of California's kelp forests that cleans parasites off other fish and sleeps buried in sand.

entities.name: Spanish hogfish
entities.fact: The Spanish hogfish is a purple-and-yellow Caribbean wrasse whose juveniles work as cleaners on larger fish.

entities.name: Mediterranean parrotfish
entities.fact: The Mediterranean parrotfish is the only parrotfish in the Mediterranean, prized by the Romans, and is spreading north as the sea warms.

entities.name: Bullethead parrotfish
entities.fact: The bullethead parrotfish is one of the most common Pacific parrotfish, with a blunt bullet-shaped head and a green male phase.

entities.name: Creole wrasse
entities.fact: The creole wrasse is a purple Caribbean wrasse that, unlike most wrasses, feeds in schools on plankton high above the reef.

entities.name: Slippery dick
entities.fact: The slippery dick is a common Caribbean wrasse named for its slimy, hard-to-hold body; it changes from a striped female to a greener male.

entities.name: Angelfish
entities.fact: Marine angelfish are flat, brilliantly coloured reef fish with a sharp spine on the gill cover, and many look completely different as juveniles than as adults.

entities.name: Butterflyfish
entities.fact: Butterflyfish are thin, disc-shaped reef fish, many with a false eyespot near the tail to confuse predators, and many pair for life.

entities.name: Blue tang
entities.fact: The regal blue tang was made famous as Dory; it can lock its blade-like tail spines out as a defence and plays dead when frightened.

entities.name: Yellow tang
entities.fact: The yellow tang is a bright lemon-yellow surgeonfish from Hawaii, one of the most popular marine aquarium fish; Hawaii now breeds them in captivity.

entities.name: Emperor angelfish
entities.fact: The emperor angelfish of Indo-Pacific reefs is striped blue and yellow as an adult, but its juvenile is dark blue with white rings, so different it was once thought a separate species.

entities.name: Queen angelfish
entities.fact: The queen angelfish of the Caribbean wears a blue 'crown' ringed with spots on its forehead and feeds mostly on sponges.

entities.name: French angelfish
entities.fact: The French angelfish is black with golden scale edges, mates for life and often approaches divers; its juveniles clean parasites from other fish.

entities.name: Copperband butterflyfish
entities.fact: The copperband butterflyfish has a long snout for picking food from crevices and a false eyespot on its dorsal fin; aquarists use it to eat pest anemones.

entities.name: Raccoon butterflyfish
entities.fact: The raccoon butterflyfish has a black mask across its eyes like a raccoon and feeds at night on coral polyps and small animals.

entities.name: Powder blue tang
entities.fact: The powder blue tang is a pale blue surgeonfish with a black face and yellow dorsal fin, found on Indian Ocean reefs, often in large grazing schools.

entities.name: Flame angelfish
entities.fact: The flame angelfish is a small, fiery red-orange dwarf angelfish with black bars from the Pacific islands, a prized aquarium fish.

entities.name: Longnose butterflyfish
entities.fact: The longnose butterflyfish, or forcepsfish, uses its tweezer-like snout to pick tiny animals from coral crevices; it is Hawaii's lauwiliwilinukunukuoioi.

entities.name: Threadfin butterflyfish
entities.fact: The threadfin butterflyfish has a trailing thread on its dorsal fin and a chevron pattern on its sides; it is one of the most widespread Indo-Pacific butterflyfish.

entities.name: Foureye butterflyfish
entities.fact: The foureye butterflyfish of the Caribbean has a large false eye near the tail, so predators strike at the wrong end.

entities.name: Naso tang
entities.fact: The naso tang, or orangespine unicornfish, has bright orange tail spines like a lipstick, and the males trail a long filament from each tail lobe.

entities.name: Regal angelfish
entities.fact: The regal angelfish, striped in orange, white and blue, is a shy sponge-eater of Indo-Pacific reefs that is notoriously difficult to keep in aquariums.

entities.name: Sohal surgeonfish
entities.fact: The sohal tang of the Red Sea is a striped surgeonfish with bright orange tail blades that it uses fiercely to defend its territory against divers and other fish.

entities.name: Achilles tang
entities.fact: The Achilles tang is a black surgeonfish with a teardrop of bright orange around its tail blade, living in the surge zone of Pacific reefs.

entities.name: Convict tang
entities.fact: The convict tang is a pale surgeonfish with black bars like a prisoner's uniform that grazes in huge schools that overwhelm territorial damselfish.

entities.name: Sailfin tang
entities.fact: The sailfin tang raises enormous dorsal and anal fins to look twice its size, and is banded brown and yellow.

entities.name: Coral beauty
entities.fact: The coral beauty is a hardy dwarf angelfish, purple-blue with an orange belly, that is one of the most commonly kept marine angelfish.

entities.name: Rock beauty
entities.fact: The rock beauty is a Caribbean angelfish, yellow at the front and black behind, that feeds mainly on sponges.

entities.name: Gray angelfish
entities.fact: The gray angelfish is a large, drab Caribbean angelfish that often follows divers; its juveniles are black with yellow bars.

entities.name: Longfin bannerfish
entities.fact: The longfin bannerfish is a black-and-white butterflyfish with a long white dorsal banner, often mistaken for the Moorish idol.

entities.name: Masked butterflyfish
entities.fact: The bluecheek butterflyfish is a lemon-yellow Red Sea butterflyfish with a blue-black patch over its eye, usually seen in pairs.

entities.name: Koran angelfish
entities.fact: The koran angelfish gets its name from the arabesque markings on the tail of some adults, said to resemble Arabic script; juveniles are blue with white arcs.

entities.name: Clarion angelfish
entities.fact: The clarion angelfish lives only around Mexico's Revillagigedo Islands and Clipperton, where it cleans parasites from giant manta rays.

entities.name: Masked angelfish
entities.fact: The masked angelfish lives only on the deep reefs of the Northwestern Hawaiian Islands and is pure white with a black mask as a female.

entities.name: Kole tang
entities.fact: The kole tang, or goldring bristletooth, is a Hawaiian surgeonfish with a gold ring around each eye and comb-like teeth for brushing up algae and detritus.

entities.name: Potter's angelfish
entities.fact: Potter's angelfish is a dwarf angelfish found only in Hawaii, orange with blue-black scribbles.

entities.name: Tinker's butterflyfish
entities.fact: Tinker's butterflyfish is a deep-reef butterflyfish from Hawaii, white with a bold black triangle, so rare that it fetches high prices from aquarists.

entities.name: Lined butterflyfish
entities.fact: The lined butterflyfish is the largest butterflyfish, growing to about 30 centimetres, with thin vertical lines and a black band through the eye.

entities.name: Atlantic blue tang
entities.fact: The Atlantic blue tang is a Caribbean surgeonfish that is bright yellow as a juvenile and turns deep blue as it grows.

entities.name: Peppermint angelfish
entities.fact: The peppermint angelfish, striped red and white, lives on deep reefs in the Cook Islands below 100 metres; one at Hawaii's Waikiki Aquarium drew offers of 30,000 dollars.

entities.name: Red snapper
entities.fact: The northern red snapper of the Gulf of Mexico can live for over 50 years and is so popular that many cheaper fish are passed off as it in restaurants.

entities.name: Goliath grouper
entities.fact: The Atlantic goliath grouper can reach 2.5 metres and over 300 kilograms, and makes a booming sound to warn off divers.

entities.name: Nassau grouper
entities.fact: The Nassau grouper gathers in huge spawning groups at the same Caribbean sites each winter full moon, which made it easy to overfish; it is now endangered.

entities.name: Black sea bass
entities.fact: The black sea bass of the US east coast starts life as a female and later changes into a male with a bright blue hump on its nape.

entities.name: Giant grouper
entities.fact: The giant grouper, or Queensland grouper, is the largest bony fish on coral reefs, reaching about 2.7 metres and 400 kilograms.

entities.name: Coral trout
entities.fact: The coral trout is a red, blue-spotted grouper of the Great Barrier Reef, not a trout at all, and the most valuable fish in Queensland's reef fishery.

entities.name: Striped bass
entities.fact: The striped bass, or striper, runs from the sea up rivers to spawn and is the state fish of several US states; it was introduced to the Pacific coast in 1879.

entities.name: Yellowtail snapper
entities.fact: The yellowtail snapper of the Caribbean has a yellow stripe running into a deeply forked yellow tail and often hovers in midwater above the reef.

entities.name: Grey snapper
entities.fact: The mangrove snapper, or gray snapper, grows up among mangrove roots and is one of the most commonly caught snappers in Florida.

entities.name: Mutton snapper
entities.fact: The mutton snapper is a large Caribbean snapper with a black spot on its side and blue lines on its face, prized for the table.

entities.name: Red grouper
entities.fact: The red grouper of the Gulf of Mexico digs and maintains pits in the seabed that become homes for many other reef animals.

entities.name: Black grouper
entities.fact: The black grouper is a large grouper of the western Atlantic, growing to about 1.5 metres, with rectangular dark blotches on its sides.

entities.name: Gag grouper
entities.fact: The gag grouper is the most commonly caught grouper off Florida's Gulf coast, a grey fish with wavy markings that forms spawning groups offshore.

entities.name: Cubera snapper
entities.fact: The cubera snapper is the largest snapper in the Atlantic, reaching over 1.5 metres, with thick canine teeth like a dog's.

entities.name: Dusky grouper
entities.fact: The dusky grouper is the big grouper of Mediterranean rocky reefs, a favourite of divers in marine reserves after decades of spearfishing made it scarce.

entities.name: Coral hind
entities.fact: The coral hind is a vivid orange-red grouper covered in bright blue spots, common on Indo-Pacific and Red Sea reefs.

entities.name: Red hind
entities.fact: The red hind is a small Caribbean grouper with red spots that gathers to spawn at traditional sites and is a staple catch in the Virgin Islands.

entities.name: Lane snapper
entities.fact: The lane snapper is a pink-and-yellow striped Caribbean snapper with a black spot on its side, common on grass flats and reefs.

entities.name: Schoolmaster snapper
entities.fact: The schoolmaster is a yellow-finned Caribbean snapper that gathers in daytime schools beneath elkhorn coral and mangroves.

entities.name: Vermilion snapper
entities.fact: The vermilion snapper, or beeliner, is a slim red snapper relative of the southeastern US that often ends up sold as red snapper.

entities.name: Giant sea bass
entities.fact: The giant sea bass of California can reach over 2 metres and 250 kilograms, and nearly vanished before fishing for it was banned in 1982.

entities.name: Kelp bass
entities.fact: The kelp bass, or calico bass, is a mottled sea bass of California's kelp forests and one of the state's most popular sport fish.

entities.name: Humpback grouper
entities.fact: The humpback grouper, or panther grouper, is a polka-dotted, small-headed grouper that swims head-down and is farmed as a luxury fish in Asia.

entities.name: Warsaw grouper
entities.fact: The Warsaw grouper is a huge grouper of deep rocky ledges in the western Atlantic, reaching over 2 metres, with an unusually tall second dorsal spine.

entities.name: Snowy grouper
entities.fact: The snowy grouper lives on deep rocky bottoms of the western Atlantic; its juveniles are dotted with white spots like snow.

entities.name: Speckled hind
entities.fact: The speckled hind is a deep-water grouper of the southeastern US, dusted with tiny white spots, so overfished that it is now protected.

entities.name: Tiger grouper
entities.fact: The tiger grouper is a Caribbean grouper with diagonal tiger stripes that visits cleaning stations to have its gills picked clean by gobies.

entities.name: Orange-spotted grouper
entities.fact: The orange-spotted grouper, or estuary cod, is a brown grouper with orange spots that is farmed widely in Southeast Asia for live-fish restaurants.

entities.name: Two-spot red snapper
entities.fact: The two-spot red snapper, or bohar, is a big Indo-Pacific snapper that forms massive spawning schools, and its flesh sometimes carries ciguatera poison.

entities.name: Wreckfish
entities.fact: The Atlantic wreckfish, or stone bass, is a big deep-water sea bass whose young shelter under floating wreckage and driftwood.

entities.name: Chalk bass
entities.fact: The chalk bass is a tiny Caribbean sea bass, barely 8 centimetres long, that is both male and female at once and takes turns laying eggs with its partner.

entities.name: Potato cod
entities.fact: The potato cod is a grouper of the Indo-Pacific covered in large dark blotches like potatoes; the tame giants of the Cod Hole on the Great Barrier Reef are famous among divers.
